questions.prompt: What is the difference between an anagram and a palindrome?
options: Both must have the same meaning as another word
Anagrams rearrange letters; palindromes read the same in reverse
questions.explanation: An anagram changes an arrangement while keeping all the letters. A palindrome keeps the same letter sequence when it is reversed.

title: Palindromes: LEVEL has a neat little secret
practice: Enjoy spotting a hidden rule? Try Connections.

sections.html:
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. It can be a word, a phrase or a number, as Merriam-Webster explains. Here we are playing with letters.

Read LEVEL from left to right. Now start at the other end: L, E, V, E, L. You arrive at exactly the same word. There is a satisfying little click when you notice it.

RADAR and CIVIC do the same trick. They do not need to mean similar things. The rule is about the order of their letters.
sections.title: A word that refuses to change

sections.html:
You can check a long word without trying to pronounce it backwards. Compare its first and last letters, then move one place inwards.

In LEVEL, the two outside letters are L. The next pair is E. The V sits on its own in the middle. Every pair matches.

Try the same check on LEVER. It nearly looks right, but the first L and last R disagree immediately. One mismatched pair is enough to break the rule.

This is letter symmetry, rather than a claim that every printed letter looks identical in a mirror. The spelling stays the same when its order is reversed.
sections.title: Start at the edges

sections.html:
Try “Never odd or even.” For this phrase puzzle, ignore spaces, punctuation and capital letters. That leaves NEVERODDOREVEN.

Its letters read the same in either direction. The spaces will land in different places if you reverse the original sentence, so it matters that we agreed on the rule first.

Now try “Step on no pets.” Write just its letters and compare the two ends, working towards the middle.

Check the phrase

STEPONNOPETS reads the same backwards. S matches S, T matches T, and the remaining pairs match too.
sections.title: Can a whole sentence do it?

sections.html:
Anagrams ask, “Can I rearrange these letters?” Palindromes ask, “Does reversing their order change anything?”

CAT → ACT passes the first test. RADAR passes the second. Sharing letters is not enough to make a palindrome.

Finish with a small hunt: which of LEVEL, LEVER and LEMON survives being read backwards? Then find a shorter example you might call a family member.

One possible answer

LEVEL survives. MUM and DAD are short palindromes too. The other two words change when reversed.
sections.title: Two puzzles, two questions

description: Read LEVEL backwards and it refuses to change. Meet words that work in both directions, then try a sentence with the same little trick.
